title: Why Most Managers Fail: Avoid These 5 Deadly Mistakes
author: Gaurav Jain
summary: Gaurav Jain argues that most managers fail not for lack of intelligence or work ethic but because they repeat a small set of avoidable mistakes. He opens with survey figures suggesting that companies frequently promote the wrong people and that many new managers fail within two years. The article then walks through five failure modes: micromanaging, avoiding tough conversations, tolerating low standards, taking credit while passing blame, and neglecting team development. For each, Jain diagnoses the underlying motive, often fear of failure or discomfort, and prescribes a corrective behavior paired with a named framework such as Situational Leadership, Radical Candor, SMART goals, Servant Leadership or the GROW model. His closing claim is that great managers are built through awareness, intention and reflection rather than born.
points: Jain frames micromanagement as fear of failure in disguise, arguing that control kills innovation and drives the best people out, and recommends shifting from control to coaching.
Avoiding difficult conversations is presented as a failure of accountability rather than kindness, because letting performance issues slide signals that low standards are acceptable.
Tolerating mediocrity tells top performers their extra effort does not matter, which the author argues causes them to leave quickly.
Sharing credit for success and owning failure is treated as the basis of trust, captured in the line that success should be shared and failure shouldered.
Developing people is cast as a manager's own responsibility rather than HR's, because neglecting it dries up the pipeline of future leaders.
quotes: Sure, you think you’re keeping the team on track, ensuring everything’s done your way. But truth be told— that’s not leadership, it’s control.
The irony? Your constant need to hover over every detail is probably because you’re afraid of failure. But micromanagement is the fastest way to ensure exactly that.

If you’re avoiding difficult conversations, you’re failing as a leader. You think you’re being nice and respectful of people’s feelings, but what you’re actually doing is breeding mediocrity and resentment. When you let performance issues slide or sugarcoat feedback, you’re signaling to your team that low standards are acceptable.

Think about the message you’re sending when you let things slide: “Good enough is good enough.” Is that the standard you want your team to live by? Because when you tolerate mediocrity, you’re telling your top performers that their efforts don’t matter — and they’ll leave.

When you steal the spotlight, you’re telling your team their efforts are invisible. And when you pass the blame, you’re showing that you value your own reputation more than the truth. This creates a toxic environment where no one feels safe to take risks or push boundaries.
If you’re only focused on execution in the short-term, you’re missing the bigger picture. You’re not just leading a team for this quarter — you’re building the future leaders of your organization.

Leadership isn’t about being perfect — it’s about being aware. These five mistakes — micromanagement, avoiding tough conversations, setting low standards, taking credit, and neglecting development — can become your silent killers if you are unaware.
